title: Apéry Technique for ζ(5) — Irrationality Framework
description: Formalizes the irrationality criterion underlying Apéry's 1978 proof that ζ(3) is irrational, and provides a conditional theorem: IF Apéry-type integer approximation sequences exist for ζ(5), THEN ζ(5) is irrational. The open problem is constructing such sequences.

meta.author: formalized in Lean 4
meta.assumptions: 0 sorries, 0 axioms. All theorems are fully proved. The main results — apery_criterion, geometric_decay_tendsto, and all conditional theorems — contain no mathematical assumptions beyond the hypotheses stated.

overview.historicalContext: Roger Apéry's 1978 proof that $\zeta(3)$ is irrational stunned the mathematical world. At age 61, Apéry presented at the Journées Arithmétiques conference a sequence of identities that produced integer sequences $(a_n, b_n)$ satisfying $b_n \zeta(3) - a_n \to 0$ geometrically — fast enough to prove irrationality by a simple denominators argument. Henri Cohen reconstructed the proof on the spot; several attendees left in disbelief. The method rests on a 3-term recurrence $(n+1)^3 u_{n+1} = (2n+1)(17n^2+17n+5)u_n - n^3 u_{n-1}$ with remarkable integrality properties. Despite decades of computer searches, no analogous recurrence is known for $\zeta(5)$. Zudilin (2001) showed at least one of $\zeta(5), \zeta(7), \zeta(9), \zeta(11)$ is irrational via a different method, but cannot identify which one.
overview.problemStatement: Can Apéry's method be extended to prove $\zeta(5)$ irrational? Concretely: do there exist integer sequences $(p_n, q_n)$ such that $q_n \cdot \zeta(5) - p_n \to 0$ with $q_n \cdot \zeta(5) - p_n \neq 0$ for all $n$? This file proves that the existence of such sequences would imply $\zeta(5)$ is irrational, and formalizes the abstract criterion.
overview.proofStrategy: The core mathematical content is the **Apéry Irrationality Criterion**: if integer sequences $(p_n, q_n)$ approximate $\alpha$ so that $q_n \alpha - p_n \to 0$ but $q_n \alpha - p_n \neq 0$, then $\alpha$ is irrational. The Lean proof proceeds by contradiction: if $\alpha = r \in \mathbb{Q}$ with denominator $d > 0$, then $q_n r - p_n = (q_n a - p_n d)/d$ where the numerator is an integer. Since $q_n r - p_n \neq 0$, the numerator is nonzero, so $|q_n r - p_n| \geq 1/d > 0$ for all $n$ — contradicting $q_n r - p_n \to 0$. The file then packages this criterion into the `AperyWitness` structure and proves the conditional theorem for $\zeta(5)$.
keyInsights: The irrationality criterion is purely topological: any real $\alpha$ with a sequence of nonzero integer linear combinations tending to 0 must be irrational. This follows from the discrete nature of $\mathbb{Z}$: nonzero integers have absolute value $\geq 1$, giving a positive lower bound $1/d$ on $|q_n \alpha - p_n|$ when $\alpha = a/d$.

Lean's `Metric.tendsto_atTop` provides the key bridge: `Tendsto f atTop (nhds 0)` is equivalent to the $\varepsilon$-$N$ definition, allowing extraction of an $N$ with $|f(N)| < 1/d$ — contradicting the lower bound.

The `AperyWitness` structure separates the mathematical criterion from its application: `tendsto_zero` is the convergence hypothesis, `never_zero` ensures the approximations are not exact rationals. Constructing such a witness for $\zeta(5)$ is the open problem.

For $\zeta(3)$, Apéry's sequences achieve geometric decay at rate $r = (\sqrt{2}-1)^4 \approx 0.029$, giving superpolynomial convergence. The `StrongAperyWitness` structure captures this quantitative form, with `geometric_decay_tendsto` proving that geometric decay $|f(n)| \leq C r^n$ with $r < 1$ implies convergence to 0.

The obstruction for $\zeta(5)$: extensive computer searches by Zagier, Zudilin and others have found no 3-term polynomial recurrence producing Apéry-type sequences. The method likely requires higher-dimensional structures (multiple polylogarithms, Padé approximants in several variables).

sections.title: Part I: The Apéry Irrationality Criterion
sections.summary: Proves apery_criterion: if integer sequences pₙ, qₙ satisfy qₙ·α - pₙ → 0 with qₙ·α - pₙ ≠ 0, then α is irrational. The proof uses the discrete lower bound |q·α - p| ≥ 1/d for rational α with denominator d.

sections.title: Part II: Abstract Apéry Witness Structure
sections.summary: Defines AperyWitness α bundling the convergence and never_zero conditions. Proves apery_implies_irrational: any α with an AperyWitness is irrational.

sections.title: Part III: ζ(5) Conditional Theorem
sections.summary: Defines zetaFive as the infinite series ∑ 1/n^5 and proves zetaFive_irrational_if_apery_witness: the existence of an AperyWitness for ζ(5) implies ζ(5) is irrational.

sections.title: Part IV: Geometric Decay
sections.summary: Defines HasGeometricDecay structure (rate < 1, constant C, bound |fₙ| ≤ C·rⁿ). Proves geometric_decay_tendsto using squeeze_zero_norm and tendsto_pow_atTop_nhds_zero_of_lt_one. Defines StrongAperyWitness with a geometric rate and provides StrongAperyWitness.toAperyWitness conversion.

sections.title: Part V: Apéry's ζ(3) Recurrence as Template
sections.summary: States Apéry's explicit recurrence for ζ(3), defines IsAperyTypeRecurrence as the general form, and states OpenProblem_ζ5_Apery as the existence question for a StrongAperyWitness for ζ(5).

conclusion.summary: The file fully proves the Apéry irrationality criterion (0 sorries, 0 axioms) and packages it into a framework ready for application to ζ(5) — the moment integer approximation sequences are found, the conditional theorem immediately yields irrationality.
conclusion.implications: The formalization makes the mathematical gap precise: the irrationality criterion is provable from basic topology and arithmetic, while the construction of Apéry-type sequences for ζ(5) remains open. The `AperyWitness` structure provides a specification that any future proof of ζ(5) irrationality via this method would need to satisfy.
openQuestions: Does an `AperyWitness` exist for $\zeta(5)$? Equivalently: are there integer sequences $(p_n, q_n)$ with $q_n \zeta(5) - p_n \to 0$ and $q_n \zeta(5) - p_n \neq 0$? This is the key open problem.
Does a `StrongAperyWitness` (geometric decay) exist for $\zeta(5)$? Computer searches up to high order have found no such sequences, suggesting the Apéry method may not extend to $\zeta(5)$ at all.

Could a different irrationality proof strategy (e.g., the Ball-Rivoal approach, multiple zeta values, or as-yet-unknown methods) bypass the need for Apéry-type sequences and prove $\zeta(5)$ irrational directly?
